channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The Senate considers permitting reform.
item.dc:creator: Will Kaback
item.description: Plus, a question about Samuel Alito and the Supreme Court.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Senate permitting bill. On Monday, November 16, the Senate voted 70–27 to end debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a major permitting reform bill. The decision sets up a final Senate vote on the legislation, and if passed, it would then go to the House. The 494-page bill would constitute the most comprehensive permitting reform in decades, significantly overhauling existing processes for building projects that require federal approval. 

Back up: Federal permitting for building projects is primarily regulated by environmental protection statutes enacted throughout the 1960s and 70s. As time has passed, delays to major building projects — including clean-energy developments — have become more common, prompting calls for reforming the process. BAAJA comes after months of bipartisan negotiation in the Senate and was introduced by Democratic and Republican senators on the Environment and Public Works and Energy and Natural Resources committees.

BAAJA would significantly reform four existing statutes: the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the Clean Water Act (CWA), and the Endangered Species Act (ESA). In each case, the bill would limit the existing law’s scope when it comes to reviewing and denying permits for new building projects; BAAJA’s changes attempt to preserve core environmental protections while removing more restrictive provisions. It additionally includes provisions that would hinder the executive branch’s ability to block permits; streamline the process for approving transmission lines; digitize the federal permitting process; and reform processes for hydropower, offshore energy, hardrock mining mill sites, and geothermal and nuclear energy projects.

On November 7, the bill’s sponsors released a manager’s amendment to the bill, giving Native American tribes greater determinative power in many of the suggested reformed processes; the amendment also clarified language in the bill’s permitting certainty section.

President Trump, energy developers and labor unions have expressed support for the bill; however, climate groups largely oppose it. Democrats are split, with some arguing lawmakers should delay action until Democrats assume large majorities in both chambers of Congress next year.

Below, you’ll hear views on the bill from the right and the left. Then, Senior Editor Will Kaback’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • The right supports the bill, with many expecting it to expedite projects.
  • Some argue BAAJA offers strong bipartisan solutions.
  • Others criticize climate activists for resisting permit reform.

The National Review editors called the bill “a golden opportunity for permitting reform.”

“Republican lawmakers have long sought to ease permitting for fossil-fuel production, while Democrats have wished to do the same only for clean energy. They joined for the rare congressional deal that improves matters in both directions,” the editors wrote. “If Republicans had drafted the legislation alone, they likely would have included more provisions from their 2023 legislation aimed at expanding oil and gas production.

“Yet compromise is a political necessity for any lasting reform effort, and to the extent the Senate has moved the ball forward on permitting, it has done so overwhelmingly toward deregulation and growth,” the editors said. “For once, Congress has taken initiative and done serious work to improve the nation’s laws… When they return from the midterm elections, lawmakers will have an elusive opportunity to clear roadblocks for infrastructure and energy projects of all sorts. They should seize it.”

In Cato at Liberty, Travis Fisher and Michael Abi-Nader said “America’s private sector is ready to build.”

“BAAJA builds on previous reform efforts, such as Manchin-Barrasso’s EPRA in 2024 and this term’s SPEED and PERMIT Acts,” Fisher and Abi-Nader wrote. “This moment is different for myriad reasons — electricity demand growth is reaching levels not seen this century, costly Biden-era energy subsidies have mostly been cut or curtailed, and Democrats now understand how much damage a president can inflict when he despises certain forms of energy.”

“And the stakes are high. Consulting firm McKinsey estimated in 2025 that up to $1.5 trillion in infrastructure investment was awaiting federal permits,” Fisher and Abi-Nader said. “BAAJA is an excellent set of bipartisan reforms. Not perfect by any means, but a substantial movement in the right direction. Our question to policymakers is this: Will you embrace reform, or will the federal government continue to deny permission for much-needed energy projects?”

In the Daily Caller, David Blackmon suggested the bill “would put [advocacy] groups out of the problem-creating business.”

“The Natural Resources Defense Council, the Sierra Club and a swarm of allied activist groups are trying to kill the most serious permitting reform bill Congress has taken up in years,” Blackmon wrote. “They oppose it because it would shrink the bureaucratic rot and litigation veto that keep them in business. It is no surprise these conflict groups oppose a bill which would help resolve conflicts. These groups exist to preserve and extend conflicts, not to solve them.”

“The conflict groups could not stop the first vote. They are now trying to peel Democrats off before final passage... and to park the bill until January. The country cannot afford that delay. American energy demand is rising in every part of the economy,” Blackmon said. “[The bill] would put real deadlines on reviews… limit the lawsuit treadmill used to stop projects, and require data centers to pay their own way. That is why the bill needs to become law.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left is mixed, with some saying the legislation removes important environmental protections.
  • Some celebrate the bill’s potential to enable future renewable energy projects.
  • Others express concern that BAAJA gives President Trump too much power.

In CounterPunch, Katie Bilodeau said BAAJA will “[remove] much of the remaining protective measures.”

“BAAJA is described as ‘permit reform,’ which simply means it amends environmental laws,” Bilodeau wrote. “This isn’t just about energy projects. The bill would amend environmental laws themselves, including any project proposed for public land or that uses a significant amount of taxpayer money. Think of logging projects, fish-poisoning projects, or roadbuilding projects as well as mining projects.”

“BAAJA presumes that all government decisions are good, so they should be hard to challenge and the decision should remain in force, even if laws were broken to get there,” Bilodeau said. “Bills are inherently value-driven. Proclaiming that S. 5653 ‘cuts red tape’ clarifies that the real driving value is to eliminate current environmental protections, which would allow our government to authorize environmental damage with little accountability.”

In The New York Times, Ezra Klein argued “leaving the system unchanged is a guarantee of calamity.”

“I don’t want this column to read as more confident about this bill than I really am… Legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect,” Klein wrote. “But at its core, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would do the same thing over and over again: It would make it faster and simpler to build energy infrastructure by rolling back the opportunities for delays, lawsuits and vetoes that have proliferated in recent decades.”

“The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand… with renewables. What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels,” Klein said. “I don’t dismiss the concerns any [Democrats] have about this bill. But it’s a risk worth taking to make the future they’ve promised possible.”

In Common Dreams, Dean Baker suggested returning to permit reform “after Trump is gone and democracy is restored.”

“I have long been familiar with the argument for permitting reform and am largely in agreement,” Baker wrote. “But I still can’t buy Ezra Klein’s enthusiastic endorsement of the bill [in] the New York Times over the weekend. The point is that the bill will substantially reduce opportunities to block energy- and infrastructure-related projects. That is a great idea, but not with Donald Trump in the White House and picking the projects.”

“[Trump] has already said that he will deny permits to wind turbines, apparently due to a hatred resulting from their placement near one of his golf courses in Scotland. It’s a safe bet that Trump will do everything in his power, and then some, to block the development of clean energy in his last two years in office,” Baker said. “The framing of this as a short-term ‘affordability’ story, as Klein does, is Washington-silly.”

My take.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
 
  • I’ve grown accustomed to legislative inaction, so a major bipartisan bill like this gives me some hope. 
  • Critics of BAAJA have valid concerns, but the bill’s trade-offs are worth it. 
  • Passing the bill may build sorely needed policymaking momentum in Congress.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Since I began writing for Tangle, I’ve spent many a take bemoaning legislative inaction as the executive and judicial branches assert more and more power. So today, I’m glad (excited, even) to be writing about a bill that’s not only ambitious and bipartisan, but has a strong chance of becoming law, too. Congress is doing something! Best of all, I think it’s doing something good.

Let’s start with the central premise of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA): Infrastructure permitting processes in the U.S. are too slow, expensive and fragmented, making it harder to meet energy needs and driving up prices for consumers. Consider a few examples of how difficult it has become to build energy projects in the United States. According to an Energy Department report, “The number of miles of newly built high-voltage transmission has declined… from an average of 2,500 miles each year from 2013–2015 to just 56 miles in 2023.” And 2021–2024 was the slowest four years of high-voltage transmission line construction since at least 2010. Berkeley Lab’s Queued Up report found that at the end of 2025, roughly 8,200 projects were actively seeking grid interconnection in the U.S. 

Meanwhile, the median time to complete the environmental impact statements mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) was 2.8 years from January 2019 to December 2024 (somewhat humorously, that’s an improvement of five months compared to 2010–2018). And while NEPA was designed (in part) to compel federal agencies to consider the environmental impacts of their decisions, some experts have found that these requirements actually bog down renewable energy projects that environmental advocates champion.  

The horror stories caused by the current system are everywhere — a “fast-tracked” power project that was finally approved after 17 years, a wind farm project that was abandoned after 16 years, a natural gas pipeline that didn’t start operating for six years after construction began. It’s a mess, and as writers on the right and left agreed upon above, unwinding the tangle of environmental reviews, disparate agency requirements, and complex approval processes is imperative for the U.S. to meet rising energy demand (and keep costs in check). 

Hearteningly, both sides also agree on a key piece of that reform. The bill would empower the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve new interstate transmission lines when proposals hit snags at the state level, along with a slew of other provisions to expedite new builds and upgrade existing ones. As National Review’s editors noted (under “What the right is saying”), the reforms would also remove barriers to emerging energy sources like geothermal and hydropower, bolstering an all-of-the-above energy policy. 

I could spend the rest of this take writing about other provisions I like in BAAJA, like accelerating nuclear power adoption and protecting consumers from higher energy bills linked to new data center construction. But its limitations are just as important to discuss. 

Legal scholar Steve Vladeck made the strongest argument I’ve read against passing the bill in its current form. He highlights how BAAJA would remove or weaken key legal remedies for potential violations of environmental laws while making it harder for courts to review or undo federal agencies’ permitting decisions. It would restrict the president’s ability to block already-approved permits, but also empower them to prioritize their preferred projects. That puts enormous power in the president’s hands. 

Currently, that’s President Trump, who has two more years in office and is eager to sign BAAJA into law. His critics are sounding the alarm that the bill would allow him to spend his remaining time blocking clean energy projects (and greenlighting new fossil fuel development). The president has a tendency to rush certain projects on dubious legal grounds, and this law could further embolden him. Conversely, a hypothetical Democratic president in 2029 could spend the next four years sidelining new (and necessary) fossil fuel projects and boosting “green energy” in ways that enrage the right. You can see the dilemma for both sides. Are we really fixing the permitting system if we just open it up to presidential whiplash every four or eight years, creating new uncertainty for developers and eliminating legal pathways to constrain executive overreach?

Environmental concerns loom large over this debate. A bill that seeks to introduce efficiency and order to permitting processes sounds great on paper, but what if some of the “inefficiencies” existed for good reason? For instance, if a proposed project could create environmental hazards for a community or pollute a waterway or disrupt a local economy, maybe we shouldn’t be speeding through its approval process. A more methodical approach, while frustrating at times, offers a buffer against decisions that could harm people and the environment. 

Ultimately, these concerns don’t convince me to oppose the bill. Many of its critics suggest that it would destroy all meaningful environmental review and enable unchecked pollution — that isn’t the case. The bill changes NEPA, but it doesn’t eliminate it. Environmental impact statements are still required, agencies will still have to consider the environmental risks of proposals, and regulations are still in place to curb air and water pollution. The timelines for those processes will be accelerated and certain considerations removed, but projects will still face considerable scrutiny before winning approval. 

Even still, some of the concerns I flagged could be addressed by holding the bill through the lame-duck session and taking it back up with the Democratic Congress in the new year. But getting to this point took months of hard negotiations, and I think it’s far from guaranteed that Republicans would maintain their support if the bill stalled out now. Furthermore, the ultimate travesty would be allowing fear of what President Trump (or any future president) might do to scuttle reforms with so much potential. 

BAAJA’s trade-offs are worth it. Realizing a future of more robust, sustainable, and affordable energy projects involves taking risks, and this bill has plenty. But we have no shot at getting there with the status quo. 

Plus, don’t discount what passing BAAJA could do for our national psyche. As I wrote earlier, Congress’s inaction or indifference on so many issues has been maddening for all of my adult life. Obviously, they’ve passed some major bills in recent years, and one permitting reform bill isn’t exactly a sea change. But the legislative branch has become historically unproductive, and passing a bill like this would show that even a polarized Congress can still do things. It’d be a demonstration of competence and responsiveness at a time when it’s sorely needed. I hope lawmakers recognize this opportunity. 

Take the survey: What do you think of BAAJA? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s resignation and Nvidia’s future.
item.dc:creator: Kmele Foster
item.description: The scandal could have far-reaching consequences.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia. On Thursday, technology company Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia has hired an outside firm to investigate the claims and has faced increasing scrutiny from public officials over its business practices. Separately, on Monday, the Justice Department and Commerce Department announced that investigations into the company associated with the alleged spy have been underway since 2024. 

Back up: Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew the company into a leading developer of computer chips used for gaming, data science, high-performance computing, artificial intelligence (AI), and more. It is one of the largest companies in the world by market capitalization, with Huang serving as a widely recognized voice on AI development. 

Huang is alleged to have had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese national and business executive who joined the Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed in 2023. The company then purchased billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and came under suspicion of illegally diverting those chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. In February, Singapore barred Alice Huang from entering the country for allegedly misrepresenting her role with Megaspeed, but the country did not prosecute her for any crime or investigate her for espionage. Megaspeed has denied breaking any laws and said that Huang left the company in 2025.

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang were first photographed together in December 2023 and have been seen together in public several times since. This spring, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo to top Trump administration officials informing them that U.S. officials knew of a close relationship between the two, and that they believed Alice Huang had been recruited as a spy. President Donald Trump was also reportedly briefed on the intelligence findings in October 2025 but did not take action at the time.

In a November 8 email to Nvidia employees, Huang acknowledged having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues, though he did not address his relationship with Alice Huang specifically. Three days later, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital affair with the company’s vice president of health care; the next day, Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a different employee. Neither Nvidia nor Huang has commented on these additional allegations. 

President Trump and some tech leaders have expressed support for Huang in the wake of his resignation. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as CEO and rejected the suggestion that the relationship with Alice Huang risked U.S. national security. Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly criticized Nvidia, questioning the company’s culture and saying it requires a “dramatic shakeup” after Huang’s resignation. Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department is responsible for enforcing restrictions on certain AI chip exports to China, are traveling with President Trump to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders’ Meeting. Ahead of that trip, the administration issued an interim final rule closing a loophole that had allowed China to access advanced compute power by renting it from data centers outside the country. 

Today, we’ll have views from the left and right on the fallout from Huang’s resignation, followed by Editor-at-Large Kmele Foster’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left criticize the leadership structure of top tech companies. 
  • Some question Commerce Secretary Lutnick’s decision making. 
  • Others say Jensen Huang’s successor faces a daunting task.

In The American Prospect, Ryan Cooper argued “this is the problem with oligarchy.”

“Huang is out because, remarkably enough, Nvidia is one of the better-governed tech companies,” Cooper wrote. “That said, Huang had still made himself the center of the business in many ways. He was a quintessential Silicon Valley hero-founder, always wearing his signature leather jacket, and treated like a celebrity around the world. He reportedly had 60 people reporting directly to him, as compared to the traditional five to seven for a CEO.”

“This mess leaves multiple large question marks hanging over global society… In addition to general chaos and market panic unleashed by this scandal, it may cause a sharp decline in Nvidia’s sales, if not huge legal sanctions for violating American law,” Cooper said. “What knock-on effects might that have on the financial companies that lent the money? That’s how a financial crisis gets rolling… Hyper-concentration of markets means that one man’s sexual indiscretions can become an entire planet’s economic problem.”

In Bloomberg, Jonathan Levin suggested “questions around [Lutnick]… keep growing.”

“[Howard Lutnick] has oversight of US export control programs and has to ensure that certain goods don’t fall into the hands of bad actors or anyone posing a threat to US national security. Yet, that’s exactly what Lutnick may have allowed to happen. And Congress now rightly wants answers,” Levin wrote. “The whole situation raises many troubling questions, starting with why Lutnick didn’t crack down on Nvidia chip exports to certain countries including Singapore.”

“He’s also failed to insulate himself from financial conflicts of interest. Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now run by Lutnick’s sons, has drawn attention for multiple conflicts given the firm’s intersection with the commerce secretary’s own wallet,” Levin said. “Lutnick is going to have to account for all of this, in what promises to be closely watched congressional hearings that will explore possible betrayals of national security in the interest of self-aggrandizement.”

In Semafor, Reed Albergotti said “Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive.”

“Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement,” Albergotti wrote. “Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow.

“The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled ‘Stand with Jensen,’ and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company,” Albergotti said. “The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right suggest the saga will damage China’s AI development efforts.
  • Some call for investigations into the Trump administration.
  • Others suggest the scandal proves the U.S.’s AI dominance.

In The Spectator, Matthew Lynn suggested “China is the real loser from the Jensen Huang affair.”

“In the short term people may be impressed by the reach of [China’s] intelligence operations. It is no minor achievement to plant any agent right at the heart of one of the world’s most important companies. And yet, once all the headlines have blown over, it will have three longer-term consequences,” Lynn wrote. “Its spying operations have been sensationally exposed… China has been rumbled, and it will be trusted far less after this episode.”

“Next, it will be very hard to honeytrap any more CEOs… Finally, Nvidia will have to be a lot more careful from now on. Deals that might have been possible if the honeytrap operation had never happened will now be completely impossible,” Lynn said. “The mission has rebounded on its own authors. There is still a bitter contest between China and the United States to control the technology… China has just made it a lot harder for itself.”

In The Wall Street Journal, Peggy Noonan argued “Huang is a White House scandal.”

“It is important it not be misunderstood as a merely personal story, a private matter,” Noonan wrote. “It is a story about our national security, and it carries implications in all aspects of U.S. defense and cybersecurity. It is a story about an administration’s failure to take responsibility and stop harm, for reasons that are mysterious. And of course it is about a successful top-level espionage operation carried out against America by its foremost world challenger, China.”

“Mr. Trump was saying we have to beat China while his top AI adviser appears to have been helping China win the future,” Noonan said. “If the president knew about Mr. Huang’s situation and did nothing, that is a scandal. If U.S. intelligence figures alerted the Commerce Department there was a problem with a Chinese spy and cutout companies, and Commerce did nothing, that is a scandal… There should be public hearings and investigations to drill down to the bottom of this story and get to the truth.”

In the Daily Signal, Randy Forbes said the scandal proves “why we need American tech companies.”

“[Huang’s resignation is] the latest reminder of Beijing’s determination to get its hands on American technology,” Forbes wrote. “Much has been made about the artificial intelligence race between the U.S. and China, but less is said about the semiconductor components that go into AI. It’s estimated that 65% of China’s AI capacity will come from U.S. semiconductors by the end of next year. This is how significant the American advantage is.”

“In spite of endless Chinese IP theft and state subsidies, the U.S. remains ahead in both AI models and AI computing components. Why? In 2025, the United States had 1,953 newly funded AI companies compared with just 161 in China. This was driven by $286 billion in private AI investment, compared with a mere $12.4 billion in China,” Forbes said. “If we want to truly beat China on chips, AI, and other tech, then we know the way forward. The U.S. should make it even easier for new entrants into the tech sector.”

My take.
Kmele Foster
Editor-at-Large
 
 
  • While I maintain sympathy for Jensen Huang, his actions deserve serious scrutiny.
  • Key details of this story are still evolving, but based on what we know, Huang’s affair will have cascading consequences.
  • The biggest consequence could be losing a leading advocate for technological progress.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

I was singing bedtime songs with my kids last night when I realized I’d need to rework the take you’re reading now.

I’ve spent the past several days poring over scores of media reports and commentary about Jensen Huang’s resignation. The controversy surrounding his departure from one of the world’s most valuable companies is startling, all too familiar, and, at the same time, surprisingly unresolved. Originally, I wanted to write a biting rebuke of Jensen and his decision making. But as I sat with my kids last night, I felt a pang of sympathy for him. His children are grown — in fact, they work for the company he co-founded — but I imagined them together at bedtime years ago. And I imagined the shame I’d feel if my own children, at any age, were reading disreputable revelations about me in the press.

Like all of us, I’ve said and done things that hurt the people I care about. I’ve disappointed those closest to me. And for a period, during a particularly dark stretch, those weren’t isolated lapses. I’m grateful to have had the chance to make amends and grow from those experiences. And I’m especially grateful never to have made the sort of relationship-altering choices Jensen has now admitted to. 

But Jensen isn’t an ordinary civilian enduring some private embarrassment. He had been Nvidia’s chief executive since co-founding the company more than thirty years ago, and his foresight helped position the company to achieve unparalleled technological and commercial heights. In October, the company’s market valuation approached $6 trillion, nearly a trillion dollars more than Apple. But by the beginning of this month, The New York Times was publishing deeply reported pieces on Jensen’s affair with an alleged spy. Jensen’s resignation followed soon after, indirectly acknowledging his marital infidelity but saying nothing specific about which of his extramarital relationships he was apologizing for. 

Ultimately, Jensen is responsible for his misconduct. His actions merit serious sanction for failing in his obligations to shareholders, breaching the board’s trust, and misleading the colleagues to whom he initially denied reports of his affairs. And he’s responsible for any securities violations those failures might have caused.

Still, as I mentioned earlier, our understanding of this story is still evolving. Initial reporting presented Alice Huang as a Chinese Communist Party operative and Jensen as the target of a clandestine honeypot operation, though subsequent reporting on the intelligence community’s assessments has complicated that picture. If those allegations prove true, though, this is a major scandal with major national security implications, and reports that President Trump was briefed on the matter but failed to take serious action would describe a staggering dereliction of duty. If they don’t, the injustice of Alice Huang being framed as a foreign operative deserves acknowledgment, too.

In the meantime, tech executives, investors, and one president of the United States have publicly lobbied Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen as CEO, citing his unique abilities as a business leader, his singular importance to the development of artificial intelligence, and the imperative to maintain American dominance in the industry. An open letter signed by Nvidia employees and shareholders stresses the importance of due diligence when adjudicating allegations of corporate misconduct, warns against a rush to judgment, and notes the uncertainty surrounding some of the allegations about Alice Huang.

They’re right that much remains uncertain. But what’s clear to me is that Jensen has forfeited two of his most valuable assets: trust and credibility. 

Calls for due diligence are reasonable, but they aren’t an argument against accountability. A board’s first obligation is to the shareholders it serves, and a company’s culture is essential to keeping that relationship stable. Jensen misled the board that would be rehiring him, along with the colleagues and reporters who asked him directly about his actions. Returning him to the job without severe sanctions would tell every employee at Nvidia, and every executive watching from elsewhere, that candor with your board is optional if you’re valuable enough.

I’m also less convinced than his staunchest defenders that Jensen is indispensable. He’s an exceptional executive, and few people in American business have built more consequential products. But companies of Nvidia’s scale aren’t the work of one man, however gifted, and the engineers, researchers, and managers who built its products are still there. Apple survived the loss of Steve Jobs; Nvidia can survive the loss of Jensen Huang. Insisting otherwise badly underrates everyone else who made the company what it is (and will continue to be).

For my part, I suspect the most substantial loss here has a less direct relationship with Nvidia’s share price. Jensen is among the most persuasive public advocates for the idea that technological progress is worth wanting, not merely as a weapon in some contest with China, but as an engine of human flourishing. His pitch wasn’t always mine, but few people made the optimistic case with more authority. But that authority depends on credibility, and credibility is exactly what he’s exhausted. Whatever the board decides, Jensen can’t recover the thing that made him most valuable to determined techno-optimists like me. And his exit comes just as the doomers, cynics, and skeptics are ascendant and as a newly elected Congress decides what to do about AI and data centers. The case for progress still deserves to be made. I’m just less sure, this morning, who will make it.

Staff concurrence.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
I think the Trump administration’s role in this story deserves comparable scrutiny to Jensen Huang’s and Nvidia’s. As Kmele notes, key details are still unconfirmed (including whether Alice Huang is actually a Chinese asset), but our current understanding raises serious questions about the administration’s decisions.
 
I’ve been most attuned to the growing rift between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. In Bessent’s telling, his department (and Defense, State, and the U.S. trade representative) long supported putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist over concerns it was helping China illegally access Nvidia chips, but Lutnick resisted the idea. Bessent has now spent the past week publicly haranguing the Commerce Department, and I expect scrutiny of Lutnick’s decisions to intensify — and rightfully so.
 
The New York Times has reported on clear conflicts of interest between Lutnick’s role as Commerce secretary and the business activities of his sons at their firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which stood to benefit from a laxer approach to AI chip export controls. Even setting aside those potential conflicts, the public deserves answers on Lutnick’s reluctance to crack down on Megaspeed.
 
Separately, I agree with Kmele that President Trump’s inaction when briefed on Alice Huang and Megaspeed over one year ago represents a “staggering dereliction of duty” if confirmed. How differently would this story have played out if the administration had simply notified Nvidia of its suspicions about Alice Huang after the president was briefed? How much did the administration know about Megaspeed allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China? Why is the president still expressing support for Huang and even suggesting he should be reinstated as CEO?
 
As stunning as this story already is, we still have much to learn. I hope Congress can do its part to help find answers.

Take the survey: How do you think Jensen Huang’s resignation will affect U.S. AI development? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The nationwide ground stop.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, is dark money’s influence on politics changing?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The nationwide ground stop. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded most flights in the United States due to disruptions to air traffic control communications systems. The stop lasted for approximately five hours, causing mass flight cancellations and delays that continued through the weekend. Government officials suggested the issue originated from a router installation by a government contractor, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called on Congress to pass additional funding to modernize FAA systems. 

Back up: Before Friday, the FAA had ordered a nationwide ground stop twice in U.S. history, first after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and second in 2023 when a critical computer system malfunctioned. 

Secretary Duffy said the decision to call the ground stop was made after communication and radar systems experienced “inconsistency,” creating gaps in contact between air-traffic controllers and pilots. All of the roughly 3,500 flights in the air during the disruption landed safely. By 8:15 PM ET, the systems were stable and flights began departing again. 

In a press conference on Friday night, Duffy repeatedly described the issue as a result of outdated FAA systems and said the agency needs more funding to upgrade aging infrastructure. “This is a continual problem that we have and it should be fixed,” he said. “New hardware, new software, new telecommunication.” 

Separately, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he had seen “zero evidence” that a cyberattack caused the disruptions but that his department was still investigating. Mullin later suggested that Duffy’s ongoing efforts to upgrade the FAA’s systems “was overwhelming the older system.” However, the FAA said on Sunday that the new equipment was not responsible, reporting that its initial investigation found two potential sources for the disruption: a facility in Arkansas where government contractor L3Harris was conducting maintenance on telecommunication lines, and a radar site in Texas. 

Below are views from the right and left on the ground stop. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right argue for a complete restructuring of the FAA.
  • Others note the FAA’s problems began long before Trump.
  • Still others say that Duffy’s appeal for more money fell flat.

In The Wall Street Journal, Marc Scribner suggested “tech isn’t the FAA’s biggest problem.”

“[America’s air-traffic control system] is antiquated and in dire need of an update, but money won’t solve the fundamental problem: the Federal Aviation Administration’s obsolete institutional model, which is responsible for its crumbling infrastructure,” Scribner wrote. “The agency has a dual mandate to provide air-traffic control and regulate its safety. It depends on congressional appropriations to sustain itself.

“As a result, air-traffic control competes with other federal spending priorities, and it faces operational trade-offs between efficiency and safety. This web of conflicting interests explains why the near-constant concern about the outdated U.S. air-traffic control system has persisted for decades without resolution,” Scribner said. “Those reforms start with the recognition that air-traffic service provision and safety regulation shouldn’t be performed by the same entity.”

In PJ Media, Matt Margolis wrote “Democrats hope you forget this about the last nationwide FAA ground stop.”

“[Duffy said] he expects flights to be ‘back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving.’ Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg slammed the ground stop anyway,” Margolis said. “[Buttigieg] pretended that the Biden administration was proactive about modernizing the system… [He] had four years, a mountain of infrastructure money, and his own nationwide ground stop to learn from. If he ‘got to work,’ where are the results?”

“An August 2023 New York Times investigation found that under Biden and Buttigieg, there was a sharp rise in near-collisions at U.S. airports nationwide, with internal FAA records showing that commercial airline close calls were happening multiple times a week,” Margolis wrote. “Democrats left behind a crumbling air traffic system, and now they want to prosecute the people trying to fix it.”

In The New York Post, Michael Goodwin argued “money alone won’t fix the FAA.”

“The most troubling consistency of both the press conferences on Friday and Saturday was the officials’ eagerness to blame Congress for not budgeting enough money to speed the modernization of the FAA’s communication network,” Goodwin said. “Duffy said the work should have been done years earlier, and renewed his appeal for Congress to appropriate a staggering $50 billion in new funding for emergency overhauls.

“Coming in the midst of the mysterious shutdown, the not-enough-money argument struck me as being predictable and off key. Washington is now $40 trillion in debt, or about $121,000 for each US resident. How much is enough?” Goodwin asked. “Even if Congress wrote the check tomorrow, the work would take years. So the cavalry is not coming soon. Such pleas always sound like everything would be fine if only America spent more.”

What the left is saying.
  • Some on the left expect issues with aviation systems to persist. 
  • Others question Duffy’s attempt to blame the Biden administration for the FAA’s problems.
  • Still others say the agency must be more proactive in managing risk.

In The Atlantic, Josh Tyrangiel wrote “the next major grounding will be worse.”

“Even if today has a boring explanation, the experts I’ve been talking with are pretty sure that plenty of days like this are coming, for two main reasons,” Tyrangiel said. “First, anyone can be a bad guy now… Deterrence works on parties who have something to lose and an address where you can send a reply. The trouble with AI (um, one of the troubles) is that it may hand state-grade capability to people who have neither.”

“Second, our best defense against this kind of chaos is amputation… when cyber defenders find a hole they can’t patch fast enough, the rational move is to amputate: Switch the system off and wait,” Tyrangiel wrote. “Whatever caused today’s ground stop, halting every departure in the country ‘for reasons of safety’ until someone works out what’s going on isn’t a sign that the system is failing. More and more, it is the system.”

In MS NOW, Steve Benen said the administration “tried to play a blame game.”

“Those looking to federal officials for answers were left wanting,” Benen wrote. “Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin hosted a rather clumsy, nine-minute press briefing just outside the White House, where he said very little… That led to a longer Q&A in the White House press briefing room, led by Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in which they spent roughly a half-hour explaining how uncertain they were about precisely what happened.”

“If the goal was to reassure the public, it was an embarrassing failure,” Benen said. “It wasn’t until Sunday morning when the president managed to publish a couple of brief online statements about the developments from two days earlier, and to the surprise of no one, he blamed his Democratic predecessor. For those concerned with the Republican administration’s rampant incompetence, the developments did not inspire confidence, but just as notably, Team Trump was playing a blame game it couldn’t hope to win.”

In Bloomberg, Thomas Black suggested the “disruptions need more than money to fix.”

“If you listened to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explain why flights were grounded for about four hours on Friday, you would come away thinking that a lack of funding from Congress was the culprit. That’s not the case,” Black wrote. “Duffy should have instead taken the opportunity to be frank with the American people about the challenges of upgrading the fragile infrastructure that undergirds US aviation.” 

“Voters expect critical infrastructure to function at all times, but they detest when city streets are torn up to fix a water pipe or when traffic is snarled by a highway expansion,” Black said. “Once the FAA has a better understanding of what happened on Friday and how to avoid repeating the mistake, it shouldn’t retreat into safe mode. Pushing upgrades into the future is why these antiquated systems pose such risks to air travel today. The future is now.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • The ground stop was the right call and a reminder of how fragile aviation systems can be.
  • Duffy says that more money would fix the problem, but we should rethink the FAA’s structure altogether.
  • A competitive privatization model for air traffic control would be more efficient and durable.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Consider for a moment the magnificent, outlandish miracle of modern-day air travel in America.

Nearly 45,000 flights take off and land each day, almost always without incident. At peak, some 5,500 planes are in the air at once, criss-crossing the skies at various altitudes, speeds, and directions. These flights communicate through what is essentially a giant walkie-talkie network — linked by cable lines, aided by their on-aircraft systems, and managed by air traffic controllers. Pilots can see, obviously, but a key part of flying a commercial jet is listening; they’re not just reacting to what they see out the window, but also trying to match their altitudes, speeds, and angles to the precise instructions they receive over the radio.

On Friday, some pilots and air traffic controllers noticed that those walkie-talkies were acting kind of funny. They started asking each other things like, “Can you hear that static?” or “Did you hear me calling you?” which is not exactly the sort of question you want your pilots and air traffic controllers asking while operating commercial planes full of people. The FAA, which operates under Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, began investigating the source of the communication issues — in the 45 minutes it spent trying to resolve the problem, the agency came up empty-handed while the disruptions seemed to intensify. That’s when it made the call to ground most flights.

Duffy, predictably, is now asking Congress for more money. As we speak, the FAA is trying to replace thousands of miles of copper wire with fiber optic cable to modernize its systems. Duffy said this work likely triggered Friday’s mess — a contractor completed a changeover which caused routers in the system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting feeds across air traffic control (ATC). In simple terms, the situation was akin to a four-year-old screaming “hello?!” over and over into a walkie-talkie that is communicating with all other walkie-talkies. You can see how that would make communication between pilots and ATC difficult. 

(Worth noting: Some new reporting has called Duffy’s explanation into question, and air traffic controllers have been warning about vulnerabilities in these systems for a while, but I haven’t seen a coherent alternative explanation offered, either. For now, I’m going to assume the FAA’s theory is correct.)

Here, it might be easy to dunk on Duffy as the reality TV star Transportation secretary who’s in way over his head. But the truth is Duffy is far from unusual: Of the 20 Senate-confirmed transportation secretaries since the post was created in 1967, about half had no regional or national transportation sector experience. A few were former mayors (like Duffy’s predecessor Pete Buttigieg) whose relevant experience was linked to passing legislation dealing with airports or local transit. Others had virtually no background on transportation issues at any scale. In reality, Duffy — an experienced lawyer and former congressman — has just as much government experience as many of his predecessors, even if he has much less direct transportation experience than some of them, too.

He also made the right call, which very few people seem to be saying. If my loved one was on one of the thousands of flights scheduled or in progress on Friday afternoon, I’d much prefer them getting to their destination a day late than not at all. Our risk tolerance for pilots can’t hear air traffic controllers should be quite low, and Duffy and FAA officials acted quickly and responsibly in calling for the ground stop. Friday was quite dramatic, and like everyone else, when the news broke I speculated to friends and colleagues about an Iranian attack or “AI bot gone rogue.” But similar cascading issues have surfaced repeatedly over the years, most notably in 2023 and 2009.

The question then is: Now what? 

A better solution than “keep funding the system producing poor track records” might be finally beginning the corporatization (or “utility model”) of air traffic control. This proposal would separate the FAA from ATC to make the latter a standalone public utility funded by user fees. In theory, this model would separate ATC from political volatility in appropriations and allow it to finance large-scale technology upgrades through long-term revenue bonds.

Libertarians and some conservatives have long called for the U.S. to move toward this model, and every single year their case gets more compelling (I used to be against it; now I’m not). Our system has a self-evident weakness: Fees and taxes on airlines and passengers (as well as general taxes) raise money for infrastructure improvements, and congressional appropriators then decide what to do with it rather than sending it straight to the operators. Congress gives the money to the FAA, which ends up as both referee and player — it receives the money to build out and modernize, then oversees its own use of that money. All of this happens on Congress’s timeline (through appropriations).

Over the years, Congress and the transportation sector have had spurts of momentum to reform this system. As Reason Foundation Transportation Policy Director Robert Poole noted, from 2013–2018, reform bills to move our system to a public utility model garnered support from “all the major passenger and cargo airlines, [the labor union representing air traffic controllers], unions representing pilots and flight attendants, six former U.S. Department of Transportation secretaries, all three former chief operating officers of the Air Traffic Organization, 13 former senior Clinton administration officials, transportation experts from a long list of noted think tanks, taxpayer and consumer groups, and the editorial boards of many leading newspapers, including the Chicago Tribune, Miami Herald, Orlando Sentinel, The Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, and USA Today.” 

And it’s no wonder.

Countries with strong safety regulators like Germany, the United Kingdom and New Zealand have all set up a kind of separate, fee-funded company for air traffic control. Our northern neighbor Canada has perhaps the most unique system of all — a nonprofit with a 15-person board that finances itself through aviation user fees. 

This model has improved safety and substantially lowered costs. Airlines and flyers, not the general taxpayer, fund Canadian air traffic control, and that has made efficiency a top priority. That copper wire replacement we’ve been working on for 25 years? Canada completed most of its own in 18 months under the Nav Canada system.

Success wouldn’t be guaranteed or linear, of course. Nav Canada’s entire air traffic control covers about 9,000 flights per day, a fraction of U.S. volume. As former Rep. Steve Russell (R-OK) once said, comparing the two systems is like “comparing an apple to a horseshoe.” We’re also already handing some ATC duties off to corporate America with mixed results. In fact, the defense contractor L3Harris was the group behind the repairs on Friday that allegedly triggered Friday’s nationwide grounding. 

Still, it’s not like Canada operates a completely different system with completely different vehicles. Recreating its success is a simple matter of scale, and I sincerely doubt we are incapable of following through if we really want to. But the current Transportation secretary or president is clearly far less relevant than the system itself. The FAA’s job should be to regulate — not operate — and a push to keep the agency in its lane while building out a private air traffic control system would generate more money to support the system, more efficiency in using funds, and faster modernization across the board. It’s time to stop doubling down on the FAA’s convoluted structure and start laying the groundwork for an altogether reimagined and better system. 

Take the survey: What do you think of the “utility model” proposal for air traffic control? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The failed impeachment of Pete Hegseth.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, how will congressional Republicans handle being in the minority?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The failed impeachment of Pete Hegseth. On Tuesday, the House voted 211–204 to refer eight articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee. The Republican-controlled committee is not expected to take further action, effectively ending the impeachment attempt. 11 Democrats were absent from the vote, which allowed Republicans to pass the referral measure and avoid a floor vote on impeachment. 

Back up: Impeachment is the process through which Congress can remove certain members of the executive and judicial branches from office. First, a simple majority in the House must vote to impeach. Representatives’ impeachment motions can be referred to committees for further investigation, review, and debate before returning to the House floor for a vote. If the House votes to impeach, the Senate can hold a trial and remove the official from office with a two-thirds majority vote. However, the committee can also choose not to take action. The most recent impeachment of a Cabinet member was President Joe Biden’s Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024; the Senate dismissed those charges. 

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) filed the impeachment resolution. Articles I through III accused Hegseth of illegally launching and continuing the Iran War. Article IV alleged Hegseth ignored laws that are designed to minimize civilian casualties in his decisions on Iran. Article V argued that U.S. strikes against alleged drug boats constituted extrajudicial killings. Article VI accused Hegseth of using his office to suppress Sen. Mark Kelly’s (D-AZ) free speech. Article VII concerned the extradition of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, alleging that it was an illegal kidnapping. Article VIII accused Hegseth of starting an illegal war in Yemen.

Republican leadership originally worried that the impeachment would advance due to poor attendance among their party. However, the House GOP ultimately had fewer absences than Democrats after several members said they missed the vote due to a traffic incident around the Capitol building. 

Democratic leaders have not said whether they will attempt to impeach Hegseth again in 2027, after large House and Senate Democratic majorities will be sworn in. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (NY) did not commit to any action. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said. 

Many Republicans celebrated the result of the vote. “Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” President Donald Trump said. “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”

Today, we’ll share perspectives from the left and right on the attempt to impeach Hegseth. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left supports Hegseth’s impeachment, with some doubting his defense.
  • Many criticize Massie’s strategy in drafting the articles of impeachment. 
  • Others expect Trump to stand by Hegseth for the time being.

In The Intercept, Nick Turse argued “none of it is true.”

“Over half an hour, [Hegseth] declared every military operation he has overseen ‘lawful’ and claims of civilian harm ‘slander.’ He said the Iran war was a great victory and only 18 Americans have died in the conflict. He also claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just ‘one disgruntled congressman,’” Turse said. “Experts in the laws of war, a Pentagon official, and members of Congress from both parties say Hegseth’s boat strikes against ‘cartels,’ which have now killed upward of 240 people, are illegal extrajudicial killings.”

“Of the Iran war, Air Force Lt. Col. Rachel VanLandingham, a former chief of international law at U.S. Central Command, said the opening strike ‘clearly violates the U.S. Constitution and the War Powers Resolution,’” Turse wrote. “The American people, writ large, appear to agree with Ansari, Massie, the U.S. officials, and those in the military’s orbit. Just 32 percent of voters approve of the way Hegseth is handling his job, while 57 percent disapprove.”

In Slate, Jim Newell wrote about “how Pete Hegseth escaped.”

“Hegseth may have been the ripest political target for impeachment. But these articles weren’t written to maximize votes,” Newell said. “Most Republicans have issues with Hegseth… [but] don’t have a problem with what Hegseth has done in Venezuela, or Yemen, or to people in the Caribbean, or his creative interpretations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Most of them support most of that. 

“And even though many don’t like that they lost their elections over high gas and other input prices sparked by the Iran war, they’re not outright opposed to confronting Iran,” Newell wrote. “Massie was asking them not merely to impeach Hegseth; he was asking them to reject the foreign policy of Trump’s first two years. They weren’t about to take that leap on either the policy or the politics. Even retiring members.”

In CNN, Stephen Collinson suggested “Trump is defending himself.”

“Deep into President Donald Trump’s news conference Monday, it became obvious why he’s so adamant in backing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth amid an impeachment storm,” Collinson said. “To jettison the former Fox News anchor now would be to admit that the Iran war — of which Hegseth is the administration’s most vehement proponent — was a mistake. A sacking would also undermine Trump’s attempt to recast what is at best an inconclusive military adventure and at worst a strategic disaster.” 

“If Trump rejected the man who rebranded the Pentagon the ‘Department of War,’ he’d be trashing his own brand,” Collinson wrote. “[Hegseth] seems safe from being ejected from office in the short term, since a two-thirds majority to convict seems unlikely in any Senate impeachment trial… [But] Hegseth could prove to be a liability when Trump needs to get defense spending requests through a Democratic Congress.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right question the legitimacy of the articles of impeachment.
  • Some suggest Trump might have turned on Hegseth if he hadn’t been targeted. 
  • Others argue that Hegseth is a political liability.

In Townhall, Horace Cooper said “the impeachment circus comes for the Pentagon.”

“The Framers designed impeachment as an emergency safeguard against treason, bribery, and personal corruption — not as a parliamentary vote of no confidence when lawmakers dislike a president’s foreign policy,” Cooper wrote. “Massie’s resolution… If Congress believes the executive branch has overstepped its constitutional bounds in Iran or the Caribbean, the Constitution already gives lawmakers a decisive, unambiguous tool: the power of the purse.” 

“What Congress should not do is scapegoat a subordinate Cabinet secretary for following lawful directives issued by the elected Commander in Chief,” Cooper said. “Oversight is a vital congressional duty. But turning constitutional impeachment into a tool for lame-duck political theater weakens the presidency, undermines civilian control of the military, and invites endless partisan retaliation the next time power changes hands.”

In The Free Press, Eli Lake asked “did the impeachment threat just save Pete Hegseth?”

“Normally, the prospect of a cabinet secretary’s impeachment would be a reason for a president to cut him loose. In the case of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the threat of impeachment is one very big reason why he will stay in his post at the Pentagon, at least for now,” Lake wrote. “Defending Hegseth makes sense from a political standpoint… Seven of the eight articles in Massie’s impeachment bill directly implicate the president.”

“The irony is that, without the impeachment, Trump and his allies may have found it more convenient to cut Hegseth loose at this point in his term,” Lake said. “The lasting effect of the impeachment gambit may be pushing Trump to defend a member of his cabinet associated with an unpopular war that a segment of his base deeply opposes. Massie has forced the president’s hand and, at least for now, Hegseth will likely survive because of it.”

In The American Conservative, Jude Russo made a “political argument against Pete Hegseth.”

“Let us remember that Hegseth has not been an optimally competent and PR-neutral official, even before he started howling for blood on live television. His Defense Department has been a staffing clown-show, largely self-inflicted; his high-profile reprisals against staffers, some of whom were his longtime friends and allies, in the end turned on entirely baseless accusations of leaking,” Russo wrote. “Hegseth has been a liability machine from the start.”

“Why not pin this stupendously unpopular, difficult to resolve war on him? This is obviously an argument of expediency, not justice (mostly),” Russo said. “There is an endangered official very publicly attached to a very unpopular policy. The president is no stranger to writing off distressed assets. Why not Hegseth? By his own admission, the war is why the GOP lost midterms… It should be underlined that this need not change policy; even a boring secretary of defense will do what he is told to do from on high.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • The past week has brought Democrats back to Earth after their historic midterm performance.
  • The absent Democrats’ excuses don’t add up, and their colleagues are right to be furious. 
  • I’m unsure if Hegseth deserved impeachment, but I think the process would have forced him to be more transparent and accountable.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Welp, the honeymoon is over.

Nine days ago, Democrats were basking in the glow of sweeping electoral fortunes that only come along once or twice in a lifetime. Now it’s back to reality.

Consider what’s happened since last Tuesday’s “blue tsunami.” President Trump tapped Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, the clearest signal yet that he’ll double down on maximizing executive power and lean into culture wars with the left. A few days later, House Republicans tapped Rep. Jim Jordan (OH) to replace House Speaker Mike Johnson (LA) and be their minority leader in the next Congress. Jordan has a near-zero record of passing legislation or whipping votes for leadership (his talent has been organizing votes against leadership), and he’s best known for combative hearings, dressing down Democrats in public, and punchy TV hits. Like the Miller appointment, this is a true “wartime” pick akin to replacing Sherlock Holmes with Jack Reacher. 

Meanwhile, Republicans in the Senate approved a “sense of conference” resolution that pledges to maximize their remaining days in power, attempt to pass another reconciliation bill in the lame duck session, and confirm every judicial nominee and executive nominee they can before January 3 (Republican voters might be wondering where that energy was over the last few months). The White House counsel then sent an overt threat to incoming Democrats that pursuing investigations targeting the Trump administration could be considered criminal, an assertion equaled in its boldness only by its ridiculousness. Trump also scored a major 8–1 win at the Supreme Court, which cleared his administration to continue border wall construction in West Texas, a reminder for Texas Democrats that their wins last week can’t make all their problems disappear.

And how are Democrats wielding their incoming power? Well, on Tuesday Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) argued that if Sen. Chuck Schumer runs unopposed for majority leader, Democrats should withhold quorum and deny the caucus enough members to hold its leadership vote until he presents a clear plan for the path forward with members’ input. That’s probably music to the ears of many Democratic voters who want fresh leadership, but it’s also a reminder that plenty of intraparty battles are around the corner despite the sizable majorities Democrats will enjoy next year.

Which brings us to the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote.

This was Democrats’ first post-midterm opportunity to hold the administration’s feet to the fire, and they really couldn’t have picked a better foil. The Democratic base despises Hegseth. Not to mention, he has drawn harsh criticism from former Defense secretaries and members of the military across party lines. He’s the face of a deeply unpopular war. He is openly loathed by several sitting Republican senators. He’s defended extrajudicial boat strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific that have plausibly killed innocent people. And he was facing articles of impeachment that were brought by a Republican member of Congress. 

Politically, this should have been a layup: I have argued since he was nominated that Hegseth was one of Trump’s worst cabinet picks, an underqualified leader who has a track record of controversy and poor management. I believe his tenure has affirmed that view. Regardless of whether you think impeachment is justified, demanding greater transparency and accountability about the status of the Iran war, the boat strikes, and other conflicts abroad all feel in-bounds to me. I was hoping to see him face some scrutiny.

Of course, given Hegseth’s record, more Republicans than just Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) should have been willing to advance these articles. But all Democrats had to do was show up for the vote, advance the articles of impeachment, and set up weeks of public hearings and media attention on one of the Trump administration’s least popular and most vulnerable Cabinet members — and then, maybe, the Senate would vote to remove him, a historic rebuke.

Yet they couldn’t manage the most basic function of their job.

11 Democrats (and seven Republicans) missed the vote, allowing a successful motion to refer the articles to the House Judiciary Committee and effectively killing the effort until the new Congress convenes. The absentees included some notable figures like Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-CA), once considered the most shrewd operator in the House, whose staff said she was in California receiving a lifetime achievement award (congratulations, I guess?). Also absent was Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI), who became a household name a couple of weeks ago after endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race (she hasn’t explained the absence, but reportedly spent the day before hiding out in the Republican cloakroom). 

Reps. Jonathan Jackson (D-IL), Melanie Stansbury (D-NM), Laura Gillen (D-NY), Marilyn Strickland (D-WA), and Brittany Pettersen (D-CO) each claimed that they missed the vote because of a D.C. traffic jam, which would have been a pretty mediocre excuse on its own. 

Yet it turns out that at least Rep. Jackson was lying. 

TMZ reporter Charlie Cotton saw Jackson on the Capitol steps recording a social media video about Hegseth’s impeachment while the vote was happening, a series of events that sums up this moment in history better than anything I could write here. When Don Lemon confronted Jackson with the timeline, the representative conceded that he had made a mistake, messed up his times, and would take accountability for his actions. Inspiring stuff.

Meanwhile, the Democrats who moved heaven and earth to be there were rightfully infuriated. Rep. Pat Ryan (D-NY) underwent back surgery on Monday and checked himself out of the hospital on Tuesday morning to make the vote. A seething Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA) told MeidasTouch Network on Tuesday night that Democrats “should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.” By Wednesday morning, according to The New York Times, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-MA) was lambasting party members in a closed-door meeting for squandering the opportunity.

One way to read the last 10 years of U.S. politics is that Donald Trump was elected in 2016 to burn down the status quo. By 2020, voters realized they didn’t much like the alternative and turned to elder statesman Joe Biden to guide the U.S. out of the pandemic. His stewardship produced some very unpopular economic outcomes, which allowed Trump to pull off a remarkable political comeback in 2024. Now, two years into his second term, it appears Americans are remembering what it’s like living under his leadership and not much liking that, either. So once again, voters are wielding their power — and we just got a crystal-clear reminder of how a president can suffer a devastating rebuke of his leadership even while the opposition party remains historically unpopular. 

Democrats were just handed a generational opportunity to rebuild their coalition. That doesn’t start in January — it started this week. And if it’s true that you never get a second chance to make a first impression, the party is already playing from behind with the American public.

Take the survey: Do you think Hegseth will eventually be impeached? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

Under the radar.

This week, the Associated Press reported that 1,156 schools closed during the last academic year, the highest total since the Covid-19 pandemic. The closures come as student enrollment numbers fall, suggesting schools could continue to shut down at an accelerated rate in the years ahead. Researchers say that the decreasing U.S. birth rate is primarily driving the enrollment decline, but recent immigration crackdowns, increased adoption of private school vouchers, and homeschooling are also contributing. Two research groups have estimated that public schools could lose $11.5 billion in annual state revenue by 2030–2031 if enrollment trends continue. The Associated Press has the story.

item.title: Trump says U.S. will end Israel aid.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, how Veterans Day came to be.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

U.S. aid to Israel. On Tuesday, November 3, President Donald Trump announced that U.S. aid to Israel will end at the start of 2027, saying that the country “no longer need[s] it.” The president said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought the idea to him years ago, and the two agreed that now is the time to end the assistance. While Trump indicated that the roughly $3.8 billion in annual aid would be reduced to zero, recent reporting from Israeli outlets suggests the package will only be halved as a result of shortening its time frame. 

Back up: The United States has provided Israel with approximately $300 billion in combined economic and military aid since Israel’s founding. As part of that assistance, the Obama administration signed a memorandum of understanding in 2016, agreeing to send $3.8 billion annually through 2028. The majority of the aid goes to purchases of U.S. military equipment and services; weapons sales are subject to Congressional review, but Congress has never blocked a transfer. 

In his comments on Tuesday, President Trump suggested that the annual aid payments were an effective political target for the left. “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen,” he said. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like [Democratic Senate candidate Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” 

In January, Prime Minister Netanyahu said he wanted to “taper off” U.S. aid to Israel in the next decade. On Friday, he said Trump’s decision to end the annual assistance “shows the strength” of the relationship, adding, “Israel has a strong and stable economy.” 

While President Trump suggested that the aid would end in its entirety in 2027, Israeli news outlets Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported this week that a new memorandum of understanding would continue the aid for five years through 2033, after which it would be phased out completely. The White House has not shared further details on the plan. 

The developments come as political leaders in both parties have scrutinized the U.S.–Israel relationship amid protracted conflicts in the Middle East, including Gaza and Iran. Today, we’ll share views from the right, left, and Israeli writers on the potential aid cutoff. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take. 

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right question when the aid cut will be implemented.
  • Others say the decision won’t change progressives’ criticism of Israel.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board said the leaders “discussed phasing it out over years, not months.”

“President Trump’s Election Day surprise that he will end aid to Israel is less and more than meets the eye. Less because he is acting on a proposal of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and joint plans that have been in the works for at least a year. More because of what the move says about the worsening politics of the U.S.–Israel relationship,” the board wrote. “Mr. Trump came around to the Netanyahu idea; if Israel no longer wanted aid, why force it?

“Discussions advanced to phase out the aid over several years, starting at the end of 2026. That’s why the President’s statement on Tuesday that it would all end in two months caught Israelis unaware. Did Mr. Trump misstate the point? Or did he deliberately put it in the way he felt would be most politically advantageous?” the board asked. “This augurs poorly for the Jewish state, even if it would rather tear off the Band-Aid with Mr. Trump… than have a hostile Democratic President end aid as punishment after 2028.”

In National Review, Noah Rothman suggested “cutting off Israel won’t appease the ‘anti-Zionist’ left.”

“The president’s approach to this issue has a domestic political component. ‘Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like [Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it?’ Trump asked. ‘It’s a bad talking point,’” Rothman wrote. “If this becomes U.S. policy at the beginning of next year, as Trump forecast, it will have about as much effect on the anti-Israel left’s advocacy as did the end of high-tempo combat operations inside Gaza 13 months ago. Which is to say, it won’t have any effect at all.”

“Those who continue to rail against the ongoing ‘genocide’ inside Gaza are operating independently of the facts on the ground. Why should an amendment to a line item that consumes 0.05% of America’s annual outlays represent a moderating force?” Rothman asked. “There are many compelling reasons to transition away from the current posture toward Israel on which both sides of the equation can agree. But mollifying Israel’s monomaniacal critics isn’t one of them. They cannot be appeased.”

What the left is saying.
  • Some on the left suggest the political costs of aid aren’t worth it for Israel.
  • Others say the U.S.’s relationship with Israel is evolving.

In Vox, Eric Levitz wrote about “the Israeli case against U.S. aid to Israel.”

“Trump’s remarks Tuesday morning seem to have been ad-libbed. The Israeli Treasury Department reportedly had no knowledge of a supposed joint agreement to end U.S. aid. And existing U.S. law provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual funding through 2028. All this said, Trump didn’t pluck his Election Day rant out of thin air,” Levitz wrote. “Rather, his remarks actually reflect a prominent strain of thinking among Israeli leaders and security experts. 

“In their view, America’s cash may no longer be worth the political blowback that it invites,” Levitz said. “A voter doesn’t need to have any strong opinion about the Israel–Palestine conflict to oppose sending billions of dollars to a wealthy foreign country… On the U.S. left, right, and center, political winds are blowing against aid to Israel. With some of that country’s own leaders and admirers bowing to such gusts, the draw down of American aid to Israel might now be a matter of when, not if.”

In MS NOW, Zeeshan Aleem said “the foreign policy script is flipping.”

“Trump remains under fire for joining forces with Israel in an unpopular war with Iran, and his Tuesday statement sounded like a Hail Mary attempt to help the GOP win over swing voters who oppose aid to the U.S. ally,” Aleem wrote. “If that particular aid package is ended, it’s likely to be replaced by a more covert policy of arming Israel with U.S. weapons. But Trump clearly recognized that it could be politically advantageous to appear to be severing aid to Israel. 

“A slow-moving but seismic shift is taking place across American politics: Progressives are gaining real power in the debate over Israel,” Aleem said. “For decades, the conventional wisdom has held that criticizing Israel too forcefully is politically lethal. But Trump saw an Arab American progressive like El-Sayed as a threat to the GOP’s voter base because he criticized Israel. We seem to be in the early stages of an inversion of the bipartisan consensus on support for the longtime ally.”

What Israeli writers are saying.
  • Many Israeli writers note that aiding Israel also benefited the U.S.
  • Others say Israeli leaders must better justify the decision to end the assistance.

In JNS, Duvi Honig suggested “aid to Israel was also Israel’s aid to America.”

“U.S. President Donald Trump’s announcement about ending approximately $4 billion in annual U.S. military aid to Israel has people worried, as though Israel just suffered a terrible financial loss,” Honig wrote. “My reaction is exactly the opposite: Thank You, Hashem! It’s all for the best. For decades, Israel has been giving America extraordinary strategic, technological, intelligence and economic value while being portrayed as the country standing with its hand out.” 

“How much has American research and development benefited from Israeli expertise? How many American lives and military resources have been protected through Israeli intelligence and defense technology?” Honig asked. “Perhaps what looks like a financial loss will become the beginning of greater economic independence, more opportunities for Israeli industries and a partnership that better recognizes Israel’s true contributions.”

In The Jerusalem Post, Yoram Dori called the aid “a central pillar of Israel’s national security and military planning.”

“Let us consider the facts.
